title: Looking for feedback on my AI-assisted game dev workflow
author: Same-Arm1117
selftext:
I've been building a game as a learning solo project and have gradually developed a fairly structured AI-assisted development workflow. I'm doing this mostly as a hobby to learn AI and experiment with automating different workflows, and what I've learned has actually been pretty useful in my day job as well.

I'm curious how others are approaching this and whether there are obvious ways I could make my setup more efficient.

My current workflow is roughly:

* **ChatGPT** \- creative direction support, game/system architecture, design discussions, and turning decisions into implementation tasks for Codex.
* **Codex in VS Code** \- repo-aware agent that reads the project, audits existing documentation/code, makes changes, runs validation, and reports the results back.
* **Git** \- source of truth and change history.
* **Unity** \- game implementation
* **Me** \- architecture/creative decisions and approval gates.

The basic loop works like this:

**ChatGPT Web > scoped task > Codex/VS Code Desktop > GIT repo changes + validation report > ChatGPT Web > next decision/task**

ChatGPT helps me reason through the design and prepare a scoped task. I give that task to Codex in VS Code. Codex works directly against the repository, updates the files, validates the changes, and gives me a report. I bring the results back into ChatGPT and use that to figure out the next step.

This has worked surprisingly well, but I'm wondering if there's a better way to automate or speed up the process. The biggest annoyance right now is that I'm basically the API between ChatGPT and Codex manually copy and pasting long reports between the two.

I copy the task out of ChatGPT Web, paste it into Codex in desktop VS Code, wait for Codex to work, then copy its report and paste it back into ChatGPT. Depending on the task, either one might crank away for 5–10 minutes. At that porint, I usually start start watching a YouTube while I'm waiting, come back 20 minutes later, and have to figure out which AI I was waiting on and what the hell we were doing.

I've watched a few videos about Claude Code and have considered buying a subscription to experiment with that workflow. I've held off mostly because I'm several months into GPT/Codex-assisted development and was approaching a major project milestone. My thought was to reach that milestone first and then potentially give another AI environment the existing project/repository and see how well it can pick everything up.

But I'm also not convinced switching models/tools actually solves the underlying workflow problem.

I'm not necessarily trying to build some completely autonomous software factory. I mostly want to eliminate the mechanical copy/paste and babysitting between steps.

Would love to hear how other people are handling this, especially if you've moved beyond the basic "chat with AI → copy/paste → IDE → copy/paste back to AI" workflow.

What would you change about this setup?

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body: Just run the planning in Codex rather than web. You can avoid copy paste this way.

comments.author: Robonotes1760
comments.body: Why can you not use chat in Codex for planning?

replies.author: SimCFB
replies.body: Web chat has a separate token meter. Often far more generous. You save on tokens this way.

replies.author: big_illuminati
replies.body: Ooooh. That's why I burned through so many fucking tokens last night. Jfc

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
I tried various combinations of IDE and chat window but I've just stuck with Codex for everything. It's all in one place, easy to use and the harness is obviously designed to work with OpenAI models.

I have a single orchestrator thread which then spawns sub agents as required. I put a fair amount of effort into giving the orchestrator clear guidance on how I want to work. Sol tends to get overly complicated if you don't instruct it clearly.

comments.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
comments.body: You can have multiple chats running in codex in vscode (as well as multiple agents). Sometimes what I will do is have two different sessions going and then i just jump back and forth and can tackle two problems at once. As long as they are not dependent on each other and are separated, it's totally fine.

replies.author: high_voltage_152
replies.body: Can codex inside vscode interact with editor objects like prefabs and scenes? Or you need a different integration for that?

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: I don't believe so. However, there should be solutions out there that don't require a whole lot of setup. I would just do some research if it's something you think you want/need.

comments.author: SimCFB
comments.body:
Congrats you have become what is called a "Meat proxy".

I would be careful with Astra. I haven't actually tested but I believe the amount of chat messages you get with Astra is much less than Sol. So you may actually be using more tokens not less with this approach. With Sol it made sense because the amount of chatting you could do was seemingly unlimited. Chatting with a codex agent was thus a waste. Despite codex having a much better context base. It made sense to transfer the context.

comments.author: Danknoodle420
comments.body: Just use codex for everything. Astra can be really token intensive so I'd recommend using it solely as an orchestrator for other agents. Use chat to plan, have the Astra orchestrator read those chats.

comments.author: algorys
comments.body:
Je fais un peu la même.

Mais maintenant, je fais beaucoup d'idées et de scripts prototypes sur le web. Pour déjà simuler selon les algos ce que ca donne sur X parties ou Y temps.

J'aime bien aussi faire des design dans d'autre IA pour voir si elles ont d'autres idées.

Enfin, plus chronophages mais utile aussi, je fais des croquis de mes personnages, créatures ou écran que je donne ensuite à l'IA pour l'aider a optimiser.

Le plus long est surtout les nombreux tests derrière pour tester le fobctionnel et ne pas croire que c'est parce que les tests passent que tout est OK.

comments.author: TheAuthorBTLG_
comments.body: I have automated this. I just describe the game or change in a few sentences. The agent creates tickets, which are then split up by the next agent, which are then implemented by the next wave of agents, targeted by the agents, and it's done.

replies.author: Same-Arm1117
replies.body: This sounds very close to what I'm trying to get to. What are you using for the ticket/orchestration layer and agent handoffs? Is this something you built yourself, or are you using an existing framework/tool? Also curious how you handle human approval gates before downstream agents continue.

replies.author: TheAuthorBTLG_
replies.body: It's a homemade specialized ticket system. There's one specific status called "Human Review Needed".

comments.author: IslandProducer
comments.body: Install Beads and point them both to it.

comments.author: OldManUDC
comments.body: My opinion is that the web chatbot window is doing something to maintain an architectural context layer for you. I like to keep hierarchical design docs , so the model can go to the feature, find a ref to the design doc, and get what it needs without blowing up its context window

replies.author: Same-Arm1117
replies.body: Ok, so it sounds like I could capture architectural context and structure in a markdown file and shift work directly to codex but have codex continue to reference the archtiectural file for structure

comments.author: IcyBother8850
comments.body: I make Codex with sol write the design spec and save it as readme inside the project. Then luna writes development stages docs with actionable tasks based on the design doc, the we implement one by one with luna, write implementation notes and also maintain a codemap documentation explaining on high level what the big classes/modules do and how they interface, then for every next task gpt has docs for context. Hope this helps.

comments.author: odragora
comments.body:
I'm doing something very similar.

ChatGPT has Google Drive integration, so I think you can automate the process through having Codex agents write to files synched with Google Drive, and then chats in the web app will have access to them, and vice versa.
